title: Alcohols
description: Link alcohol structure to oxidation, leaving-group activation, protection, and phenol redox chemistry.

cards.rule: A primary, secondary, or tertiary alcohol has one, two, or three carbon substituents on the OH-bearing carbon. Hydrogen bonding raises boiling points relative to comparable nonpolar molecules. Small alcohols mix well with water; increasing hydrocarbon size lowers water solubility. For comparable molecular sizes, additional OH groups strengthen hydrogen bonding; branching often lowers boiling point, but competing effects require actual data. In water, simple alkyl alcohol acidity generally decreases methanol > primary > secondary > tertiary: alkyl donation and poorer solvation destabilize alkoxide. Electron-withdrawing groups can lower pKa; solvent matters.
cards.cue: Count C neighbors of C–OH; do not count the number of OH groups. Name a principal alcohol with -ol (or -diol for two OH groups); use hydroxy- when OH is a prefix. On benzene, ortho, meta, para mean 1,2-, 1,3-, 1,4-.
cards.trap: A secondary alcohol is not an alcohol with two hydroxyl groups. Phenol has OH directly attached to an aromatic ring and differs in acidity from an aliphatic alcohol.
cards.app: An OH group can increase water affinity and supply a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor in a binding site, but whole-molecule properties still matter.

steps.label: 1. Secondary alcohol
steps.text: The OH-bearing carbon has two carbon neighbors and one H. It is a secondary alcohol.

challenge.prompt: Select the carbon whose neighbors determine alcohol class.

steps.label: 2. Tertiary alcohol
steps.text: Three carbon groups surround the OH-bearing carbon, which therefore has no C–H bond. This changes its usual oxidation behavior.

rule.title: Alcohol Physical Properties: Intermolecular Hydrogen Bonding, Boiling Point & Acidity

items.label: Boiling Point Hierarchy (Same MW)
items.text: Carboxylic Acid (dimer H-bonds) > Alcohol (O–H H-bonds) > Ketone/Aldehyde (strong dipole) > Ether > Alkane (dispersion only).

items.label: Chain Length & Branching Effects
items.text: Longer chains ↑ BP (more van der Waals surface) and ↓ water solubility; branching makes molecules spherical → ↓ surface area → ↓ BP.

items.label: Alcohol Acidity in Solution (pKa 15.5–18)
items.text: In water, 1° ROH (pKa ~16) is more acidic than 3° ROH (pKa ~18) because bulky alkyl groups block solvent H-bonding around the RO⁻ alkoxide!

comparison: Highest BP vs ether/alkane of same MW
Moderate BP; soluble in water only if small

figure.caption: Compare the carbon neighbors of the OH-bearing carbon. These are different illustrative alcohols.

cue.title: Boiling Point & Solubility Predictor
cue.prompt: Which physical property comparison is on the exam?

items.label: Butan-1-ol vs. Diethyl Ether (Both C₄H₁₀O)
items.text: Alcohols have an O–H bond that both donates and accepts intermolecular H-bonds; ethers lack O–H bonds and cannot H-bond to themselves.

items.label: Butan-1-ol vs. tert-Butanol (Chain vs Branched)
items.outcome: Linear Butan-1-ol Has Higher BP; t-BuOH Has Higher MP
items.text: Linear chains pack more surface area for dispersion in liquids (↑ BP), while spherical symmetry packs tightly into crystals (↑ MP).

items.label: Choosing a Base to Deprotonate ROH (pKa ~16)
items.outcome: Use NaH, Na/K Metal, or LDA (NOT NaOH Residual 100%)
items.text: NaOH (H₂O pKa 15.7) gives only an equilibrium mixture; NaH (H₂ pKa 35, evolves gas) drives alkoxide formation to 100%.

trap.title: Thinking Ethers Can Hydrogen-Bond to Themselves

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Ranking diethyl ether near butan-1-ol in boiling point because "both have an oxygen atom that hydrogen-bonds".

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Pure ethers have NO O–H, N–H, or F–H bonds: they can accept H-bonds from water, but pure liquid ether has only weak dipole-dipole forces.

app.title: TLC Silica Elution Order & Membrane Permeability of Hydroxylated Drugs

items.label: Silica Gel TLC (Polar SiO₂)
items.text: More –OH groups form stronger H-bonds to polar silica gel, giving a LOWER Rf value and slower column elution.

items.label: Phase I Hepatic Metabolism
items.text: Adding polar –OH groups increases aqueous solubility for renal excretion.

items.label: Polyol Cryoprotectants
items.text: Three –OH groups create a dense 3D H-bond network, giving high viscosity and full water miscibility.

cards.rule: Primary alcohols give aldehydes with suitable mild anhydrous oxidation (PCC is one example), or acids with suitable aqueous strong oxidation. Secondary alcohols give ketones. Tertiary alcohols do not undergo the ordinary C–H-removing oxidation without C–C cleavage. PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) under anhydrous conditions can stop primary-alcohol oxidation at an aldehyde. Jones reagent, CrO3 in aqueous sulfuric acid, or acidified dichromate commonly gives a carboxylic acid. Water allows aldehyde hydrate formation and further oxidation; reagent and conditions govern selectivity.
cards.cue: 1° → aldehyde → acid; 2° → ketone; 3° lacks the necessary C–H.
cards.trap: PCC is not the only aldehyde-selective oxidant. Do not label every reagent containing oxygen “strong enough” or assume every tertiary alcohol is inert under all conditions.
cards.app: Alcohol dehydrogenases catalyze related biological redox steps using cofactors; substrate and cofactor specificity control the result.

steps.label: 1. Locate the oxidized carbon
steps.text: Oxidizing propan-2-ol removes an O–H hydrogen and the H on its central carbon, producing C=O.

steps.label: 2. Compare the product
steps.text: The same three-carbon framework is now a ketone. Carbon–carbon connectivity is unchanged in this ordinary alcohol oxidation.

steps.label: 3. Primary-alcohol conditions
steps.text: Ethanal can be obtained from ethanol with an appropriate anhydrous oxidant. In aqueous strongly oxidizing conditions it can be oxidized further to ethanoic acid.

rule.title: Chemoselective Alcohol Oxidation: PCC / Swern / DMP vs. Jones / KMnO₄

items.label: Count α-Hydrogens on the Carbinol Carbon (C–OH)
items.text: Each oxidation step to a C=O π bond removes ONE H from oxygen and ONE H from the attached carbon (1° has 2 H; 2° has 1 H; 3° has 0 H).

items.label: Stop at Aldehyde (Anhydrous Oxidants)
items.text: PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate in CH₂Cl₂), Dess-Martin periodinane (DMP), or Swern (DMSO/(COCl)₂/Et₃N) stop cleanly at the aldehyde.

items.label: Over-Oxidation to Carboxylic Acid (Aqueous Strong Oxidants)
items.text: Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄/H₂O), Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, or hot KMnO₄ oxidize 1° alcohols all the way to carboxylic acids via the aldehyde hydrate.

comparison: 2° ROH → Ketone; Orange Cr⁶⁺ → Green Cr³⁺
Cleaves C–C bond between adjacent –OH groups

figure.caption: Secondary alcohol to ketone with a suitable oxidant; schematic, not a balanced equation.

cue.title: Instant Alcohol Oxidation Outcome Selector
cue.prompt: What alcohol class and reagent are paired in the reaction?

items.label: Primary (1°) Alcohol + PCC / CH₂Cl₂
items.text: Anhydrous conditions prevent hydrate formation, preserving the aldehyde without over-oxidation.

items.label: Primary (1°) Alcohol + CrO₃ / H₂SO₄ / H₂O
items.text: Water hydrates the intermediate aldehyde to RCH(OH)₂, which is immediately oxidized a second time to RCOOH.

items.label: Secondary (2°) vs. Tertiary (3°) Alcohol
items.outcome: 2° → Ketone (With PCC OR Jones); 3° → No Reaction
items.text: Secondary alcohols have exactly 1 carbinol H (always yield a ketone); tertiary alcohols lack a carbinol H and fail the chromate color test.

trap.title: Using Aqueous Dichromate to Make an Aldehyde or Oxidizing a Tertiary Alcohol

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Reacting butan-1-ol with Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄/H₂O expecting butanal, or oxidizing 2-methylpropan-2-ol to a ketone.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Ordinary alcohol oxidation gives a ketone from a secondary alcohol. Primary-alcohol products depend on reagent and water; tertiary alcohols lack a carbinol H for this pathway, although harsher oxidative cleavage is possible.

app.title: Breathalyzer Chromate Color Change & Hepatic Ethanol Metabolism

items.label: Classic Breathalyzer Test
items.text: Ethanol (1° alcohol) reduces orange Cr(VI) to green Cr(III) while being oxidized to acetic acid.

items.label: Ethanol → Acetaldehyde → Acetate
items.text: Alcohol dehydrogenase stops at acetaldehyde (like PCC); aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidizes it to acetate (like Jones).

items.label: Methanol / Ethylene Glycol Toxicity
items.text: Blocking oxidation prevents conversion of methanol to toxic formaldehyde/formate.

cards.rule: Converting ROH to a mesylate (ROMs) or tosylate (ROTs) gives a much better leaving group. The alcohol oxygen remains bonded to carbon during sulfonate formation. A later SN2 displacement at that carbon inverts its geometry. Acetals protect carbonyls under many basic conditions. MsCl or TsCl with a suitable base converts ROH to ROMs or ROTs. Acetal/ketal formation masks a carbonyl; these groups tolerate many bases and hydride reagents, including LiAlH4 under suitable conditions. Sulfonates are activated leaving groups, not universally inert alcohol protecting groups.
cards.cue: Activation changes what can leave. Protection temporarily changes what can react. Traditionally, an aldehyde-derived acetal carbon has H and R; a ketone-derived ketal carbon has two carbon groups. Both bear two OR groups. The broad IUPAC class acetals includes ketals.
cards.trap: Making a tosylate does not itself perform SN2 at carbon. Acetals are generally acid-labile; acid and water are needed for hydrolysis. Protection does not make a group universally inert.
cards.app: A carbonyl can be protected while another group reacts, then regenerated. Choose protection and deprotection conditions compatible with the rest of the molecule.

steps.label: 1. Sulfonate ester
steps.text: The ethyl group retains its C–O bond. The oxygen is now part of a sulfonate ester, whose leaving anion is resonance stabilized.

steps.label: 2. Ketal protection
steps.text: This ketal (a ketone-derived acetal) has two OR groups and two carbon groups at its central carbon. Acid-catalyzed reaction of a carbonyl with alcohol can form acetals or ketals; removing water favors formation.

steps.label: 3. Restore the carbonyl
steps.text: Aqueous acid hydrolyzes this ketal, regenerating the ketone and alcohol. Protection and deprotection depend on the water/alcohol balance and compatible reaction conditions.

rule.title: Alcohol Activation (Tosylates, Mesylates, SOCl₂, PBr₃) & Silyl/Acetal Protecting Groups

items.label: Sulfonate Ester Formation (TsCl or MsCl + Pyridine)
items.text: Converts poor –OH into an excellent –OTs or –OMs leaving group with 100% RETENTION of configuration because the C–O bond stays intact.

items.label: Halide Conversion Without Rearrangement (SOCl₂ or PBr₃)
items.text: Converts 1°/2° alcohols into R–Cl or R–Br with clean SN2 INVERSION—avoids the carbocation rearrangements seen with HCl/HBr!

items.label: Alcohol Protection (TMSCl / TBDMSCl or Dihydropyran)
items.text: Masks acidic/nucleophilic –OH as a silyl ether (R–OSiR₃) during Grignard/LiAlH₄ steps; deprotect selectively with fluoride (TBAF).

comparison: Oxygen attacks S; C–O bond never breaks!

figure.caption: Separate leaving-group activation and carbonyl-protection examples; these are not a reaction pair.

cue.title: Stereochemical Control: Retention vs. Inversion from a Chiral Alcohol
cue.prompt: How do you control the stereochemistry when replacing a chiral 2° –OH?

items.label: Need Net INVERSION from (R)-ROH
items.outcome: Route A: 1. TsCl/pyr (Retain) → 2. Nu⁻ (Invert) | Route B: PBr₃ (Invert)
items.text: One SN2 displacement at carbon gives net inversion: (R)-ROH → (R)-ROTs → (S)-R–Nu.

items.label: Need Net RETENTION from (R)-ROH
items.outcome: Double Inversion: 1. PBr₃ (Invert to S-RBr) → 2. Nu⁻ (Invert back to R-RNu)
items.text: Two sequential SN2 displacements at the chiral carbon invert twice (R → S → R) for net retention!

items.label: Grignard or Organolithium Fails on Halo-Alcohol
items.outcome: Protect –OH as R–OTBDMS First → Form RMgBr → Deprotect (F⁻)
items.text: Unprotected –OH (pKa ~16) instantly protonates and destroys RMgBr (conjugate acid pKa ~50).

trap.title: Inverting the Stereocenter During Tosylation (ROH + TsCl)

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Flipping the wedge to a dash when converting (R)-butan-2-ol to its tosylate ester with TsCl/pyridine.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Tosylation happens at the OXYGEN atom (O attacks S of TsCl); the chiral C–O bond never breaks during tosylation, so configuration is RETAINED!

app.title: Biological Sulfonation, Kinase Phosphorylation & Solid-Phase Synthesis

items.label: ATP Phosphorylation of –OH
items.text: Converting R–OH to R–OPO₃²⁻ turns a terrible leaving group (HO⁻) into a weak-base phosphate leaving group (HOPO₃²⁻).

items.label: Fluoride Deprotection (TBAF)
items.text: Fluoride (F⁻) selectively cleaves silyl ethers (R–OTBDMS) without touching carbon-oxygen ether or ester bonds.

items.label: HX vs PBr₃ on Neopentyl-like 2° ROH
items.outcome: HBr Gives Rearranged 3° RBr; PBr₃ Gives Clean 2° RBr
items.text: Use PBr₃ or TsCl/Br⁻ whenever you must prevent a 1,2-hydride or methyl shift.

cards.rule: Phenol is more acidic than an ordinary aliphatic alcohol because phenoxide can delocalize negative charge into the ring. Electron-withdrawing substituents can increase acidity. Hydroquinone can be oxidized to a quinone; the reverse is reduction.
cards.cue: Quinone + 2 H+ + 2 e− → hydroquinone. “Hydro” here tracks reduction, not merely adding OH groups.
cards.trap: Hydroquinone and hydroxyquinone are different terms. Hydroquinone is a reduced quinone form; a hydroxyquinone still has a quinone framework bearing an extra OH. Coenzyme Q accepts electrons upstream of complex III and delivers them to complex III. Oxidative hydroxylation to a hydroxyquinone is condition-dependent; it is not a universal second oxidation step after quinone formation.
cards.app: Ubiquinone/ubiquinol transports electrons within the mitochondrial inner membrane; proton-coupled redox chemistry links the organic structure to energy metabolism. CoQ accepts electrons from complexes I and II and passes them to III. Its isoprenoid tail keeps it in the membrane. Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone) and K2 (menaquinones) are lipid-soluble quinones with hydrophobic side chains and roles in vitamin K-dependent carboxylation.

steps.label: 1. Phenolic OH
steps.text: OH is attached directly to an aromatic carbon. Deprotonation gives phenoxide, stabilized by resonance. The pictured alternating bonds are one aromatic resonance representation.

steps.label: 2. Reduced member
steps.text: Hydroquinone has two phenolic OH groups in a para arrangement. Oxidation removes two H atoms overall, formally two protons plus two electrons.

steps.label: 3. Oxidized member
steps.text: The quinone has two carbonyls. Its ring is not simply benzene with unchanged aromatic bonding; the pi-bond arrangement has changed.

rule.title: Phenol Acidity (pKa ~10), Substituent Resonance Effects & Hydroquinone ⇌ Quinone Redox
rule.formula: Hydroquinone (Aromatic 1,4-Benzenediol)  ⇌  p-Benzoquinone (Conjugated Diketone, NOT Aromatic) + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻

items.label: Why Phenol (pKa ~10) Is 10⁶× More Acidic Than Cyclohexanol (pKa ~16)
items.text: Deprotonating phenol delocalizes the negative charge across oxygen AND the ortho/para ring carbons (4 resonance contributors).

items.label: Why Phenol Is Less Acidic Than Carboxylic Acids (pKa ~5)
items.text: Carboxylate spreads −1 charge over TWO electronegative oxygens; phenoxide spreads charge onto less electronegative carbon atoms.

figure.caption: Oxidation removes 2 H+ and 2 electrons; reverse reduction adds them. Schematic redox pair.

cue.title: Phenol Substituent Effects & Quinone Redox Recognition
cue.prompt: What phenol or quinone property is being tested?

items.label: Nitro (–NO₂) or Cyano (–CN) on Phenol Ring
items.text: Ortho and para EWGs accept the phenoxide lone pair directly by resonance + induction (2,4,6-trinitrophenol = picric acid, pKa ~0.4!).

items.label: Methoxy (–OCH₃) or Alkyl (–CH₃) on Phenol Ring
items.text: Electron-donating groups push electron density into the ring, destabilizing the negatively charged phenoxide conjugate base.

items.label: Hydroquinone / Catechol + Oxidant ([O])
items.text: Quinones are cyclic α,β-unsaturated diketones (NOT aromatic!), whereas hydroquinones ARE fully aromatic 6π benzene diols.

trap.title: Calling Quinones "Aromatic" or Extracting Phenol with NaHCO₃

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Assuming ubiquinone (CoQ) is aromatic because it has a 6-membered ring, or saying NaHCO₃ deprotonates unsubstituted phenol.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Benzoquinone has two sp² C=O carbons interrupting cyclic delocalization (non-aromatic conjugated diene-dione); phenol (pKa 10) needs NaOH (H₂O pKa 15.7), not NaHCO₃ (pKa 6.4)!

app.title: Ubiquinone (Coenzyme Q10), Vitamin K & Tyrosine Side-Chain Chemistry

items.label: Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone → Ubiquinol)
items.outcome: Q + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ QH₂ in Electron Transport Chain
items.text: Complexes I and II reduce ubiquinone to aromatic ubiquinol (hydroquinone), shuttling electrons to Complex III.

items.label: Tyrosine Side Chain (pKa ~10.1)
items.text: Deprotonated at high pH to form a nucleophile or oxidized to dopaquinone in melanin synthesis.

items.label: Vitamin E (α-Tocopherol)
items.text: Donates a phenolic H• atom to lipid peroxyl radicals, forming a resonance-stabilized phenoxyl radical.
